definition: Algorithmic bias describes the systematic and repeatable harmful tendency in a computerized sociotechnical system to create "unfair" outcomes, such as "privileging" one category over another in ways that may or may not be different from the intended function of the algorithm.
details: Bias can emerge from many factors, including intentionally biased design decisions or the unintended or unanticipated use or decisions relating to the way data is coded, collected, selected or used to train the algorithm. For example, algorithmic bias has been observed in search engine results and social media platforms. This bias can have impacts ranging from privacy violations to reinforcing social biases of race, gender, sexuality, and ethnicity. The study of algorithmic bias is most concerned with algorithms that reflect "systematic and unfair" discrimination. This bias has only recently been addressed in legal frameworks, such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (enforced in 2018) and the Artificial Intelligence Act (proposed in 2021 and adopted in 2024). As algorithms expand their ability to organize society, politics, institutions, and behavior, sociologists have become concerned with the ways in which unanticipated output and manipulation of data can impact the physical world. Because algorithms are often considered to be neutral and unbiased, they can inaccurately project greater authority than human expertise (in part due to the psychological phenomenon of automation bias), and in some cases, reliance on algorithms can displace human responsibility for their outcomes, without last mile thinking. Bias can enter into algorithmic systems as a result of pre-existing cultural, social, or institutional expectations; by how features and labels are chosen; because of technical limitations of their design; or by being used in unanticipated contexts or by audiences who are not considered in the software's initial design. Algorithmic bias has been cited in cases ranging from election outcomes to the spread of online hate speech. It has also arisen in criminal justice, healthcare, and hiring, compounding existing racial, socioeconomic, and gender biases. The relative inability of facial recognition technology to accurately identify darker-skinned faces has been linked to multiple wrongful arrests of black men, an issue stemming from imbalanced datasets. Problems in understanding, researching, and discovering algorithmic bias persist due to the proprietary nature of algorithms, which are typically treated as trade secrets. Even when full transparency is provided, the complexity of certain algorithms poses a barrier to understanding their functioning. Furthermore, algorithms may change, or respond to input or output in ways that cannot be anticipated or easily reproduced for analysis. In many cases, even within a single website or application, there is no single "algorithm" to examine, but a network of many interrelated programs and data inputs, even between users of the same service. A 2021 survey identified multiple forms of algorithmic bias, including historical, representation, and measurement biases, each of which can contribute to unfair outcomes.

explainer.lead: Algorithmic bias happens when a computer system repeatedly produces unfair outcomes, such as favoring one group of people over another. It can arise from data, design choices, or unexpected uses, and it matters because these systems influence decisions in areas including lending, hiring, healthcare, and criminal justice.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a robot choosing players for two teams, but it keeps picking children wearing red shirts even when the other children are just as good. Its choices would be unfair, and repeating them would make the unfairness a pattern. Algorithmic bias is similar: a computer may repeatedly favor one group because of the information or instructions people gave it, even if nobody meant to discriminate.
tiers.practitioner: When building or reviewing a system, examine how data was collected and coded, which features and labels were chosen, and whether outcomes repeat unfairly across otherwise similar groups. Also check design assumptions, underrepresented populations, and uses or audiences not anticipated during development. Common pitfalls include treating outputs as neutral, assuming discrimination requires intent, and expecting transparency alone to explain a complex or changing network of programs.
tiers.paperLevel: Algorithmic bias denotes systematic and repeatable errors in a computerized sociotechnical system that create unfair outcomes, such as privileging an arbitrary group of users over others; the behavior may be intentional or unintentional. NIST identifies systemic, computational or statistical, and human sources, while a 2021 survey distinguished forms including historical, representation, and measurement bias. Research is limited by trade secrecy, algorithmic complexity, changing behavior, irreproducible responses, and systems composed of many interrelated programs and data inputs.

explainer.example: Suppose a credit-score system recommends loans to one group but repeatedly denies loans to another set of nearly identical users because of criteria unrelated to their finances. Denying a loan after consistently weighing relevant financial criteria need not be unfair, but this repeatable group-based difference is algorithmic bias.

usedIn.detail: Ranking and recommendation choices can reproduce stereotypes or favor particular categories of results.

usedIn.name: Hiring, healthcare, and criminal justice
usedIn.detail: Unfair outputs can compound existing racial, socioeconomic, and gender biases.

explainer.intuition: A computer can follow its instructions perfectly and still be unfair because those instructions and their data reflect human choices and social conditions. The key issue is not a one-off mistake, but a systematic, repeatable pattern of unfair outcomes.
howItWorks: Existing cultural, social, or institutional expectations shape the problem and its data.
People collect, code, select, and categorize data, deciding what to include or discard.
Designers choose features, labels, priorities, and criteria for processing that data.
The system produces outputs that may repeatedly privilege one group over another.
Unexpected contexts, users, technical limits, or changing behavior can introduce or amplify unfairness.
explainer.whyItMatters: These systems can affect loans, school placements, healthcare, hiring, criminal justice, elections, and exposure to online hate speech. Because algorithms are often treated as neutral, their outputs may receive undue authority and obscure human responsibility for harmful decisions.
misconceptions: An algorithm is not automatically neutral merely because it follows formal instructions.
Bias does not require an intention to discriminate.
Full transparency does not guarantee that a complex or changing system can be understood.
